title: Load a dental syringe with an anaesthetic cartridge, ready for the needle
instruction: Load the syringe with the anaesthetic cartridge, ready for the needle, and leave it lying on its rest.
context: Local anaesthetic is given at most dental visits, and loading the aspirating syringe is routine chairside work for dental assistants, hygienists and dentists (about 740,000 US workers). The cartridge goes in stopper end toward the piston and the piston's harpoon is set in the stopper with a firm, controlled push, so the dentist can aspirate before injecting; much more force drives the stopper in or cracks the glass.
setup: A dental bracket table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A stainless steel set-up tray, fixed: 20 x 28 cm with a 1 mm floor and a 1.5 cm rim, from 17 to 37 cm forward and 14 cm either side of the centre line. (2) A blue silicone syringe rest on the tray, fixed: two blocks 3 x 1 x 1.6 cm, their middles 31 cm forward at 4.5 and 0.7 cm left of the centre line, each with a slot 13 mm wide and 3 mm deep across its top. (3) A breech-loading aspirating dental syringe (stainless steel, 68 g: frame 52 g, piston 16 g) lying level in the rest's slots along the left-right line, 31 cm forward, its axis 1.9 cm above the tray's floor, needle end to the left. Its barrel is 12.5 mm across with a bore of 9.4 mm, open on top along a loading window 70 mm long (from 6.5 cm left of the centre line to 0.5 cm right of it, its edges bevelled 1.5 mm); left of the window a closed front section 16 mm long and the threaded needle adapter (8 mm across, 10 mm long); right of it the barrel's back end (8 mm) with the finger grip (38 mm across). The piston, a 4 mm rod with a harpoon point 3 mm long and 1.6 mm across, runs through the back end to a soft-grip thumb ring 28 mm across (20 mm hole, 4 mm thick) lying flat, 9.5 cm behind the harpoon's point. It slides with about 1.5 N of friction and starts part way in: the harpoon 3.5 cm into the window, the ring's middle 6.5 cm right of the centre line; fully drawn back, the point is 7.1 cm from the window's front end and the ring 10.1 cm right of the centre line. (4) A stainless cartridge rack, fixed: two notched rails 8 mm wide and 10 cm long, 4.7 cm apart, across the forward line at 21.5 cm, notched at 1, 4 and 7 cm right of the centre line. (5) In the notch 1 cm right of the centre line, the anaesthetic cartridge: a 1.8 ml glass cartridge 8.65 mm across and 65 mm long (6 g with its solution), lying forward-back with its axis 2 cm above the tray's floor; at its near end a dark rubber stopper (6.85 mm across, 7.6 mm long) set 3 mm into the glass, at its far end a silver aluminium cap over a rubber diaphragm; a red drug band and a 1 mm scale printed near the stopper end. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: 0.0 if the cartridge's stopper is ever driven more than 2 mm into its glass (latched; the stopper slides in only past 35 N). Otherwise, judged at the end: 1.0 with the cartridge lying in the syringe's barrel (its axis within 1.5 mm of where it lies on the bore's floor and within 8 degrees of parallel to the barrel, wholly inside the window) stopper end toward the piston, the harpoon set, the syringe lying on its rest (its barrel down in both blocks' slots: its axis within 3 mm of where it started across and up, within 1.5 cm along, within 5 degrees of level and of the slots' line, its window up within 10 degrees) and both hands clear of it (each TCP at least 8 cm from the syringe's axis, thumb ring to needle adapter); 0.5 with the cartridge in the barrel stopper end toward the piston; 0.1 with the cartridge in the barrel the wrong way round (cap toward the piston); else 0.0. The harpoon counts as set by the scorer's aspiration test, run once the loaded syringe has lain still on its rest for 0.5 s with both hands clear: it pulls the thumb ring back 8 mm (at most 12 N; the first 5 mm may only slide the cartridge back to the barrel's back end) and back again, and the stopper must slide back at least 2 mm in its glass; the result stands while the syringe stays within 3 mm of where it was tested, the hands stay clear and the barb stays in. Real trial: the same 8 mm pull on the ring, with the stopper's travel read against the cartridge's 1 mm scale; the stopper's inset measured with a caliper before and after; the cartridge's way round, its place in the window, the syringe on its rest and the clear hands by inspection and from the video. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the syringe, its piston and the cartridge still.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). The harpoon's bite is a joint switched on when its point meets the stopper square on: the rubber pushes back like a spring (15 N at 1 mm) and gives at 15 N; the barb then holds to 40 N. The stopper slides on a stick-slip joint: in past 35 N (a sealed cartridge cracks or bursts there instead), back against a 2 N/mm vacuum spring. The window is 5 mm longer than the cartridge. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
